analysis.one_liner: Lets federal student loan borrowers refinance at current lower rates while keeping repayment protections.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill letting federal student loan borrowers refinance at lower rates was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in June 2023 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a program, run by the Department of Education within 30 days of passage, letting any federal student loan borrower apply to refinance their loan at the interest rate the government is currently offering for that loan type — fixed for the life of the loan. Borrowers would keep the same repayment term and keep credit for payments already made toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness and income-driven repayment forgiveness, so refinancing would not restart their clock. The bill would also let borrowers move older bank-held FFEL loans into the federal Direct Loan program, and require the Education Department to work with the consumer bureau to tell borrowers they are eligible.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers whose loans carry interest rates higher than what the government is currently charging — especially people with older loans that took out at rates like 6.8% — plus bank-held FFEL borrowers who would gain access to the Direct Loan program's repayment protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers with older, higher-rate federal loans

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal refinancing program that must open within 30 days of enactment, letting borrowers replace their loan with one at the rate currently offered for that loan type, fixed for the life of the loan.
Refinanced loans keep the same repayment term — no automatic extension of how long you pay — and borrowers may refinance at most twice in any 10-year period.

Payments already made on the original loan count toward Public Service Loan Forgiveness and income-driven repayment forgiveness, so refinancing does not restart the forgiveness clock; FFEL borrowers refinancing into Direct loans start that count fresh.

Borrowers with bank-held FFEL loans can have those loans paid off and converted to Direct loans, gaining access to Direct-only protections such as income-driven repayment and loan forgiveness programs.
The Education Department, working with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, must run a campaign to tell eligible borrowers they can apply, and loan servicers must pass along the information.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, which forgoes interest income by replacing older, higher-rate loans with new ones at lower fixed rates — a cost ultimately shared by taxpayers generally.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal government (taxpayers) via lower interest income

drawbacks.text: The government would earn less interest on refinanced loans, and the bill includes no offset to cover that lost revenue — it is a real cost to taxpayers, though the bill sets no estimate of its size.

Because the refinanced rate is the rate in effect on the day you refinance, a borrower holding a cheaper older loan (for example, one taken out in 2020–21 at around 3%) who refinanced while new rates were high would lock in a higher rate; the bill's 'lesser of' protection applies only to consolidation loans, not to straight refinancing of Stafford, Unsubsidized, or PLUS loans.
The program depends on borrowers learning about it and choosing the right moment to refinance; it offers no rate cut to anyone whose existing rate is already at or below the current offering.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers stuck at older, higher rates — a large share of the roughly tens of millions of federal borrowers — the bill is a straightforward monthly savings with no loss of protections, since forgiveness clocks and repayment terms carry over. The cost is lower federal interest income, which is diffuse and unpriced in the bill itself. The main design risk is timing: the rate resets to the refinance date, so borrowers with cheaper loans could harm themselves by refinancing at the wrong moment, and the bill guards against that only for consolidation loans.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Turner (R-OH) introduced the bill on June 14, 2023 with three cosponsors: two House Democrats and one House Republican, making it a bipartisan effort.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day it was introduced.
No further action was ever recorded — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal loan portfolio keeps collecting interest at older, higher rates, since no borrower got the chance to refinance. Borrowers carrying older high-rate loans — particularly on FFEL loans — continued paying those rates for another Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal loan portfolio; borrowers still pay old rates

for.name: Rep. Michael R. Turner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Student Loan Refinancing Act in the House on June 14, 2023.

for.name: Reps. Donald Norcross and Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining a Republican sponsor.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 14, 2023 and took no recorded action on it — no markup, no committee vote, no report — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with two Democratic and one Republican cosponsor — but only three members signed on, and no votes were ever taken, so the fight never took partisan shape.

industries.note: The bill lets borrowers pay off older loans held by private FFEL lenders and convert them into federal Direct loans, removing those loans from lenders' portfolios. Borrowers gain access to Direct Loan protections the FFEL loans lacked.

These companies earn fees and interest by refinancing federal loans into private loans, which strips borrowers of federal protections. A free federal refinancing option with no loss of protections undercuts their market.

Refinancing converts some FFEL loans to Direct loans serviced under the federal program, shifting servicing volume. The bill also requires servicers to distribute refinancing information to borrowers, adding work but no direct revenue change.
